main.summary: The stele tells the family history, filial conduct and career of Cao Quan, magistrate of Heyang in the Eastern Han. He put down the revolt of Hede, king of Shule, in the Western Regions and later, in the time of the Yellow Turban rising, calmed and nursed the people of Heyang, rebuilt the offices and encouraged learning. His officials and the people carved the stone to record his merit, and a verse in rhyme closes by praising his government.
main.translation:
The gentleman's given name was Quan, his courtesy name Jingwan; he was a man of Xiaogu in Dunhuang. His forebears were descended from the House of Zhou. King Wu took hold of the pivot of Heaven, cut down Yin and Shang, and when his merit was settled, blessing and emolument came together: he enfeoffed his younger brother Shuzhen Duo in the state of Cao, and from this the family took its surname. In the age of Qin and Han, Cao Shen supported the royal house. When the emperor Shizong widened the land and pushed back the frontiers, the descendants moved to the outskirts of Yongzhou and settled in different places: some in Youfufeng, some in Anding, some in Wudu, some in Longxi, and some made their home in Dunhuang. Branches divided and leaves spread, and wherever they were they were strong.

The gentleman's great-great-grandfather Min was recommended as xiaolian ("filial and incorrupt"), and served as Chief Clerk of Wuwei, Magistrate of Xunren in Ba commandery, and Commandant of Juyan in Zhangye. His great-grandfather Shu, xiaolian, served as Receptionist, Chief Clerk of Jincheng, Magistrate of Xiayang, and Commandant of the Western Section of Shu commandery. His grandfather Feng, xiaolian, served as Deputy Commandant of the Zhangye Dependent State, Chancellor of the Marquisate of Yumi in Youfufeng, Commandant of the Western Section of Jincheng, and Grand Administrator of Beidi. His father Beng had a name known through the prefectures and commanderies in his youth, but unfortunately died early, so that his rank did not match his virtue.

As a child who had just lost his milk teeth, the gentleman loved learning; he mastered the apocryphal and prognostic texts, and there was no writing he did not command. His nature of worth and filial piety grew from the root of his heart. He took in and cared for his youngest great-aunt, and served his stepmother, anticipating their wishes and carrying out their will; in his respect for the living and the dead, nothing in the rites was left out. So the villagers made a saying about him: "Doubly devoted to his elders, bringing them joy: Cao Jingwan." Through the changing of generations he carried on the virtue, and did not let his name fall. When he entered public service, his purity matched that of Boyi and Shuqi, and his uprightness followed Shi Yu. He held the senior posts of the commandery and was an Accounting Clerk; then he was summoned to Liangzhou, where he was always Assistant Governor and Chief Secretary, holding the rules and discipline of ten thousand li, where red and purple were never confused. Sent out to govern other commanderies, he impeached the crooked and corrected the wicked; the greedy and violent washed their hearts, his colleagues submitted to his virtue, and men near and far feared his authority.

In the second year of Jianning, he was recommended as xiaolian, appointed a Gentleman, and made Commandant of the Wu Section in the Western Regions. At that time Hede, king of Shule, killed his father and usurped the throne, and sent no tribute. The gentleman raised an army and attacked; he showed the humaneness of sucking an ulcer and the kindness of sharing wine. In attacking cities and fighting in the open field, his plans welled up like a spring, and his might surpassed that of the warriors named Ben. Hede had his hands bound and his face turned forward, and came to submit to death. The army returned in triumph; the states of the Regions sent gifts of courtesy worth nearly two million, all of which he entered in the official records.

He was promoted to Magistrate of Huaili in Youfufeng, but on the death of his own brother he gave up his post. Then he met with the ban on officials, and hid in the lanes of his home for seven years. In the sixth year of Guanghe he was again recommended as xiaolian. In the third month of the seventh year, he was appointed a Gentleman and made Magistrate of Lufu in Jiuquan. The evil bandit Zhang Jiao raised troops in You and Ji, and Yan, Yu, Jing and Yang rose at the same time. And Guo Jia and others, people of the county, also made rebellion, burning the city and the offices; ten thousand people were thrown into turmoil and everyone felt uneasy. Three commanderies sent word of emergency, and feathered dispatches came one after another. At that time the sage ruler consulted the officials, and all said: "It is he." So he was transferred to be Magistrate of Heyang. He gathered up the remaining embers, mowed down the scattered survivors, and cut off the root.

Then he sought out the old men and took counsel with them, and with the able elders Wang Chang, Wang Bi and others on the essentials of caring for the people; he comforted the aged and looked after widowers and widows. With his own money he bought grain and gave it to the crippled and the blind. The adult women Tao Fei and others made the medicine called "Seven Heads" and the salve called "Divine Brightness"; he went in person to the Li pavilion, and the officers Wang Gao, Cheng Heng and others handed them out to the sick, and all were healed. The flow of his kindly government was swifter than the relay post. The people came back with their children on their backs like clouds. Walls and houses were mended, markets and shops were set out in rows, wind and rain came in season, and the years brought good harvests. Farmers and weaving women and all the craftsmen bore his kindness.

In the first year of Heping the county had suffered a flood from White Thatch Valley, whose harm turned back in the north-west, and the city walls were raised. After that, the old families and the men who had cultivated themselves did not rise in office. The gentleman pitied the gentry who could not get on, and opened the south gate of the offices, facing the peak of Mount Hua, turning to the light to govern, so that scholars such as Li Ru, Luan Gui and Cheng Yin might each obtain the reward of human rank. He enlarged the hall of audience and the official buildings, the corridors and pavilions of the offices, and the steps for going up and down, for bowing and for audience. The cost did not come from the people, and the labour did not intrude on the seasons.

The Clerk of the Gate Wang Chang, the Recorder Wang Bi, the Chief Secretary Wang Li, the Clerk of the Household Section Qin Shang, the Clerk of the Merit Section Wang Zhuan and others, admiring the excellence of Xi Si and Kao Fu, together carved a stone to record his merit. The words say:

Illustrious and bright lord, his virtue and rightness shine.
He sent tribute to the royal court, and marched against the Gui lands.
His power spread and blazed, and brought peace to the strange wilds.
The army returned and came to Huaili.
Moved by brotherly feeling, he went to the mourning rites.
Alas, the rebel bandits burned the city and the market.
Specially he received the command, to mend what was ruined.
He mowed down the disloyal, and gave peace to the people.
He repaired the offices and opened the south gate.
The gate-towers stand tall, looking to Mount Hua.
Turning to the light he governed, and his kindness soaked deep.
The officers delighted in his rule, the people were supplied and content.
May the gentleman rise high, to the utmost of the three ministers' tripod.

Made on the day bingchen of the tenth month of the second year of Zhongping.

keyLines.line: 君諱全，字景完，敦煌效穀人也
keyLines.en: The gentleman's given name was Quan, courtesy name Jingwan; he was a man of Xiaogu in Dunhuang
keyLines.note: The opening gives the name, courtesy name and home of the man commemorated, Cao Quan.

keyLines.line: 時疏勒國王和德，弒父篡位，不供職貢
keyLines.en: At that time Hede, king of Shule, killed his father and usurped the throne, and sent no tribute
keyLines.note: Why Cao Quan, as Sima of the Wu section in the Western Regions, took action against King Hede of Shule.

keyLines.line: 君興師征討，有吮膿之仁，分醪之惠
keyLines.en: The gentleman raised an army and attacked; he showed the humaneness of sucking an ulcer and the kindness of sharing wine
keyLines.note: Praises Cao Quan for caring for his soldiers, as if he had sucked the pus from a wound and shared his wine with them, and so finally Hede surrendered.

keyLines.en: The rebel Zhang Jue raised troops in You and Ji
keyLines.note: The background of the Yellow Turban rising: Zhang Jue took up arms and the whole land was in unrest.

keyLines.line: 轉拜郃陽令，收合餘燼，芟夷殘迸，絕其本根
keyLines.en: He was transferred to be magistrate of Heyang, gathered the ashes of the remnants, mowed down the scattered survivors and cut the roots
keyLines.note: After moving to Heyang, Cao Quan put an end to the revolt and settled the district.

keyLines.en: The flow of his kindly government was swifter than the relay post
keyLines.note: Praises how quickly his good government spread - faster than orders carried by the post stations.

keyLines.en: Costs did not come from the people, and labour did not intrude on the seasons
keyLines.note: The building of the offices did not burden the people or take them from their farm work.

keyLines.en: Together they carved stone to record his merit
keyLines.note: Gives the reason for the stele: his officials carved the stone together to record his deeds.

glossary.note: One of the Han methods of recommending officials, in which people noted for filial piety and honesty were put forward for office.
Sucking the pus from a soldier's wound, a phrase for caring for one's men, taken from the story of Wu Qi.
Sharing wine with the soldiers, taken from the story of King Goujian of Yue.

glossary.en: Shule - an ancient state of the Western Regions
Zhang Jue - leader of the Yellow Turban rising
glossary.note: Leader of the Yellow Turban uprising at the end of the Eastern Han, which began in 184.
In today's Heyang county in Shaanxi.
Relay stations that carried orders; here a figure for how fast government orders were carried out.

main.background: The Cao Quan Stele, in full the Stele of Cao Quan, Magistrate of Heyang of the Han, was set up in the second year of Zhongping of the Eastern Han (185). Its front records Cao Quan's life and achievements. It was dug up at Heyang in Shaanxi in the early Wanli years of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644) and is now kept in the Forest of Steles in Xi'an. It is in clerical script by an unknown hand. The writing is graceful and rounded, the structure wide and flat and spreading, and the flicking strokes are clear; the style is soft and orderly. It is regarded as a model of mature Han clerical script and an important one for learning it, standing beside the Liqi Stele and the Zhang Qian Stele, each with its own style.
